title: Tariq's mountain
hook: Gibraltar is named Jabal Tariq for the commander who crossed the strait

segments.voice: Yesterday, ilm, knowledge as worship, and a look back over the age of the House of Wisdom. Your line was: a path to the garden.

A huge limestone rock stands near the southern tip of Spain, staring across a narrow strait at the mountains of Africa. Ships slide past it all day. English speakers call it Gibraltar. Say that slowly, and then say this: Jabal Tariq. By the usual account, that's where the name comes from. Jabal is mountain. Tariq is a man. So every time someone says Gibraltar, they're saying, in a worn-down way, the name of a commander who once crossed that water with an army. We leave Baghdad and go west, to al-Andalus.
screen: `A ROCK FACING AFRICA.` → `GIBRALTAR, JABAL TARIQ.` → `WEST TO AL-ANDALUS.`

segments.voice: Tariq ibn Ziyad served Musa ibn Nusayr, who governed for the Umayyads in North Africa. Tradition remembers Tariq as a Berber, one of the peoples of North Africa, and that matters: the story of al-Andalus begins with North Africans as much as Arabs. He crossed the strait with an army, landed by the rock, and marched inland. The Visigothic king, Roderic, met him in battle and was defeated, and the kingdom of the Visigoths came apart. So began Muslim rule in the land Arabic writers called al-Andalus, much of what is now Spain and Portugal. For the Christians of the Visigothic kingdom, it was a defeat and the loss of a kingdom; for Muslims, it was the start of a long chapter of life, learning and building in that land. Both memories are real, and both are kept. Then come the legends. Later histories give Tariq a famous speech to his frightened soldiers: the sea is behind you, the enemy before you. Some tellings add that he burned his ships so no one could turn back. These scenes come from later histories, and some historians treat them as legend, the kind of story that grows around a crossing that changed the map. What lasts is simpler: a man's name, carried in the name of a rock, said every day by people who've never heard of him.
screen: `TARIQ, A BERBER COMMANDER.` · `ACROSS THE STRAIT, RODERIC FALLS.` · `A DEFEAT, AND A BEGINNING.` · `THE SEA BEHIND YOU: A LATER LEGEND.` · then, large: `THE MOUNTAIN OF TARIQ.`

segments.voice: Picture two continents almost touching: Africa to the south, its mountains rising from the water, and Europe to the north, with one great rock standing at its tip. See the boats crossing, loaded with people, horses and fear, and then the same water today, ferries, fishing boats, people still crossing for every reason people cross water. If you pray, you can remember everyone who has crossed it; if not, just hold them in mind.
Tariq's mountain. Jabal Tariq, the rock named, by the usual account, for Tariq ibn Ziyad, who crossed the strait into al-Andalus. Today's word.
Your line: the mountain of tariq. A commander's name, worn into a rock. Day nine hundred thirty-three.

howItsDone: Muslim histories remember al-Andalus as a land of faith and learning, and they tell its story beginning with Tariq ibn Ziyad's crossing of the strait.
